paper_metadata.title: Effects of deviations from stoichiometry on the strength anomaly and fracture behavior of B-doped FeAl

evidence.quote: Tensile tests were conducted at temperatures ranging from 145-1123 K on four different FeAl alloys, containing 40,43,45, and 48 at.% Al, each doped with 0.12 at.% B.
An anomalous peak in the yield strength was observed in all four of the Fe-Al + B alloys studied.

Four different FeAl alloys, containing 40, 43, 45, and 48 at.% Al, each doped with 0.12 at.% B, were arc melted and drop cast into copper chill molds. Boron was added to the alloys via a master alloy, Fe-4 wt.% B.

The cast ingots (-127 mm in height and -25 mm in diameter) were canned in carbon steel billets and hot extruded at a 9 : 1 ratio. The extrusion temperatures are given in Table 1. The two alloys with lower Al contents, Fe-40Al and Fe-43A1, were originally extruded at 1073 K, but the extrusions came out cracked. The temperature was then increased to 1173 K, yielding crack-free extrusions.

The specimens were first electropolished to reduce surface irregularities and then heat treated in a vacuum of ~1 x 10^-4 Pa and furnace cooled. Heat treatment sequences for each alloy are listed in Table 1. The first heat treatment established the grain size

phases_and_microstructures.name: quenched-in thermal vacancies
phases_and_microstructures.material_state: heat treated without long-term anneal (1373 K/1.25 h + 973 K/2 h)

evidence.quote: tensile tests were conducted at temperatures ranging from room temperature to 1073 K on specimens that were given only the 1373 K/1-25 h + 973 K/2 h anneal of Table 1 (i.e. these specimens were not given the long, low-temperature, vacancy-minimizing anneal at 673 K for 120 h).
the Fe-40Al-0*12B alloy exhibited a rapid decrease in yield strength from ~430 MPa at 146 K to ~280 MPa at 473 K
the Fe-40Al-0*12B alloy exhibited a rapid decrease in yield strength from ~430 MPa at 146 K to ~280 MPa at 473 K
Above 473 K, the yield strength showed an anomalous increase with increasing temperature to a peak of ~415 MPa at 823 K.
The elongation to failure of Fe-40Al-0.12B demonstrated little change from 145 K to 473 K and then increased sharply with temperature displaying a peak of 45% at ~873 K
The valley stress, on the other hand, increases from 280 to 340 MPa as the Al concentration is increased from 40 to 45%

property_observations.material_state: heat treated without long-term anneal (1373 K/1.25 h + 973 K/2 h)

evidence.quote: First, the specimens that were not given the long-term anneal displayed higher yield strengths over the entire temperature range. Second, the strength anomaly was absent in those specimens that were not given the vacancy-minimizing anneal
Yield strength decreased from around 490 MPa at 144 K to around 410 MPa at room temperature and 473 K.

mechanisms.name: vacancy hardening
mechanisms.material_state: heat treated without long-term anneal (1373 K/1.25 h + 973 K/2 h)

evidence.quote: if present in sufficient quantity, vacancies can increase not only low-temperature strength, but also the strength at around the peak temperature
Grain-boundary strengthening is expected to dominate more at low temperatures than at high temperatures, thereby obscuring any elevated-temperature yield-strength peak.
attributed to the influence of diffusion-assisted mechanisms, such as grain boundary cavitation, which become operative at higher temperatures
Quenched-in vacancies increase the strength of the alloy at low temperatures thereby masking the yield strength anomaly.
The yield strength anomaly in well-annealed specimens may be due to the rapid increase in vacancy concentration with test temperature.
